sources.title: International House Helsinki Relocates to Pasila ‘Suomi-piste’ Service Hub
highlights: Helsinki’s one-stop service centre for newcomers, International House Helsinki (IHH), opened its doors this morning at a new address—Ratapihantie 7 in the rapidly developing Pasila business district. The relocation, effective 1 June 2026, brings IHH under the roof of the government’s brand-new Suomi-piste (“Finland-Point”) customer-service concept, which gathers multiple public bodies in a single accessible building next to Pasila rail station. IHH is best known among expatriates and global mobility teams for handling EU-citizen registration appointments, issuing Finnish personal identity codes, and providing multilingual advice on taxation, social security and local employment rules. All these services continue unchanged, but visitors now benefit from extended opening hours (09:00–16:00 Monday-Wednesday and Friday; 10:30–16:00 Thursday), barrier-free access and direct rail links to Helsinki Airport and city-centre hotels. According to the Finnish Immigration Service, the move is part of a broader digital-first overhaul of customer service. The Suomi-piste model co-locates Migri desk officers with staff from the Tax Administration, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) and the Social Insurance Institution (Kela). New arrivals can therefore register their right of residence, obtain a tax card, apply for a social-security number and receive orientation counselling in a single visit. For employers, the consolidation promises faster onboarding of foreign hires. Whereas previously an assignee might have needed three separate appointments across town, HR teams can now book one time slot through Migri’s online system and track progress via Enter Finland. Early feedback from pilot users indicates that average time-to-ID-number issuance has dropped from ten days to three. Companies should update welcome packs, relocation guides and map links immediately. The old IHH premises on Lintulahdenkuja will close permanently and no longer accept walk-in visitors. Those with appointments booked before 1 June have been automatically re-scheduled to the Pasila site, and confirmation messages have been sent to the email address on file.

# International House Helsinki Relocates to Pasila ‘Suomi-piste’ Service Hub

 Jun 2, 2026

 Finn Visas & Immigration Team @ VisaHQ

 Helsinki’s one-stop service centre for newcomers, International House Helsinki (IHH), opened its doors this morning at a new address—Ratapihantie 7 in the rapidly developing Pasila business district. The relocation, effective 1 June 2026, brings IHH under the roof of the government’s brand-new Suomi-piste (“Finland-Point”) customer-service concept, which gathers multiple public bodies in a single accessible building next to Pasila rail station. IHH is best known among expatriates and global mobility teams for handling EU-citizen registration appointments, issuing Finnish personal identity codes, and providing multilingual advice on taxation, social security and local employment rules. All these services continue unchanged, but visitors now benefit from extended opening hours (09:00–16:00 Monday-Wednesday and Friday; 10:30–16:00 Thursday), barrier-free access and direct rail links to Helsinki Airport and city-centre hotels. According to the Finnish Immigration Service, the move is part of a broader digital-first overhaul of customer service. The Suomi-piste model co-locates Migri desk officers with staff from the Tax Administration, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) and the Social Insurance Institution (Kela). New arrivals can therefore register their right of residence, obtain a tax card, apply for a social-security number and receive orientation counselling in a single visit. For employers, the consolidation promises faster onboarding of foreign hires. Whereas previously an assignee might have needed three separate appointments across town, HR teams can now book one time slot through Migri’s online system and track progress via Enter Finland. Early feedback from pilot users indicates that average time-to-ID-number issuance has dropped from ten days to three. Companies should update welcome packs, relocation guides and map links immediately. The old IHH premises on Lintulahdenkuja will close permanently and no longer accept walk-in visitors. Those with appointments booked before 1 June have been automatically re-scheduled to the Pasila site, and confirmation messages have been sent to the email address on file.

DVV Registration Finland: Get Your Henkilötunnus (2026)

# DVV Registration Finland: Get Your Henkilötunnus (2026)

DVV registration in Finland gives you a henkilötunnus (personal ID) needed for banking, tax and healthcare. It's free — here's what to bring and how to book.

At a glance

Who needs it

Foreign citizens moving to Finland on work, study, family or residence-permit grounds

Cost

Free — no fee for the henkilötunnus or municipality decision

How long

2–3 weeks (work/study) or 3–4 weeks (other cases), from your in-person visit

Where to apply

Online form at dvv.fi, then in person at a DVV service point (Helsinki, Tampere, Turku, Oulu)

You'll need

Passport/EU photo ID, residence permit or EU registration certificate, proof of grounds

Compiled by Bikram Nath from the sources listed on this page

11 min read Verified 24 July 2026

Sources include dvv.fi, infofinland.fi and muuttoilmoitus.fi. Last updated 4 November 2026; content last verified 24 July 2026.

DVV registration in Finland is how a foreigner enters the Population Information System and receives a henkilötunnus (personal identity code) that banks, the tax office and Kela rely on. You register with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency by submitting an online registration form, then attending one in-person appointment within a month. It is free and takes roughly two to four weeks.

If the henkilötunnus is the key to living in Finland, DVV registration is the lock you turn to get it. The Digital and Population Data Services Agency — DVV, or Digi- ja väestötietovirasto — is the body that enters newcomers into the national Population Information System, hands out the personal identity code, and decides whether you get a kotikunta (municipality of residence). That last decision quietly determines whether you can use a public health centre, get a Finnish ID card, or enrol a child in the local school. This guide walks through what DVV actually does, how to register as a foreigner, and the difference between simply being in the system and being a full local resident.

## How do I register with DVV in Finland?

Register with DVV in two stages: submit the free online foreigner registration form at dvv.fi/en/foreigner-registration (no authentication needed), then visit a DVV service point in person within 1 month with your passport, residence permit or EU registration certificate, and proof of work or study. Processing then takes 2–3 weeks for work and study cases, 3–4 weeks otherwise. There is no fee — the registration and your henkilötunnus (personal identity code) are completely free.

Sources: Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) — verified July 2026.

## What DVV Is and What the Population Information System Does

DVV is the Finnish government agency responsible for the väestötietojärjestelmä, the Population Information System. Think of it as the central register that every other Finnish authority reads from. According to DVV, the system stores your key personal data — names, date of birth, sex, mother tongue, citizenship, and your address in Finland — and makes it available to public authorities for purposes such as taxation, healthcare, the organisation of elections, judicial administration, and statistics.

This is the structural reason Finnish bureaucracy can feel so frictionless once you are in it. You rarely re-prove who you are or where you live, because the bank, the tax office (Vero), and the social insurance institution (Kela) all pull the same record from the Population Information System. The flip side is that until you are in that register, almost nothing else works smoothly. DVV registration is therefore not a side errand — it is the foundation the rest of your administrative life in Finland sits on.

It is worth being precise about names, because the agency has changed over the years. DVV was formed in 2020 from the former Population Register Centre and the local register offices (maistraatit), so older guides and even some employers may still refer to the maistraatti. It is the same function: the office that registers people and addresses.

## DVV Versus Migri: Who Does What

Newcomers routinely confuse DVV with Migri, the Finnish Immigration Service (Maahanmuuttovirasto). They are different agencies handling different stages, and getting the order right saves weeks.

Migri decides whether you are allowed to live in Finland. For non-EU/EEA citizens, that means granting a residence permit. For EU/EEA and Swiss citizens, it means registering your right of residence if you intend to stay more than three months. Migri is the immigration gatekeeper.

DVV comes after. Once your residence basis exists, DVV records you in the Population Information System, issues the personal identity code, and determines your municipality of residence. In practice the two can overlap — Migri often assigns a personal identity code as part of a residence-permit decision — but the population registration itself, and crucially the kotikunta decision, is DVV's job. The mental model to keep: Migri says you may stay; DVV makes you count as a resident.

## Who Needs to Register With DVV

If you are a foreign citizen moving to Finland and you meet the conditions, DVV will register your details in the Population Information System and give you a personal identity code. According to DVV, you are eligible when you are legally resident in Finland on recognised grounds, such as:

- Employment with the right to work
- Studies in Finland
- Family ties to someone already registered in Finland
- A valid residence permit (non-EU) or registration of an EU citizen's right of residence

The registration is for people who are genuinely settling in for a meaningful period, not for tourists or very short visits. If you need the code for tax reasons when you start working in Finland, a tax office can also issue a personal identity code — but that alone does not give you a municipality of residence. (For the mechanics of the code itself, see our guide to the Finnish personal identity code.)

## How to Register: The Step-by-Step Process

The process is the same regardless of nationality once your residence basis is in place. It is two stages: an online form, then an in-person visit.

### Step 1 — Submit the online foreigner registration form

Go to dvv.fi/en/foreigner-registration and complete the foreigner registration form. A useful detail: according to DVV, submitting this form does not require online authentication, so you can complete it before you have any Finnish bank credentials. If your registration involves family relationships, you submit the supporting documents at this stage.

### Step 2 — Book an in-person appointment within one month

After the form, you must visit a DVV service point in person, and you must do so within one month of submitting. The in-person step is non-negotiable — it is where DVV verifies your identity against your documents. Appointments at the busy Helsinki-area locations can fill up, so book as early as you can rather than leaving it to the end of the one-month window.

### Step 3 — Bring the right documents

Take, at minimum:

- A valid passport or EU/EEA photo ID
- Your residence permit card or EU registration certificate — or proof that you have applied for one
- Proof of your grounds for staying: an employment contract, a study certificate, or similar
- Any legalised certificates for family relationships you want recorded (marriage, birth)

Documents in languages other than Finnish, Swedish, or English may need an official translation, and foreign civil-status certificates often need legalisation (an apostille). If family registration matters to you, check DVV's document requirements in advance — this is the single most common cause of a wasted appointment.

### Step 4 — Wait for processing

Processing time, according to DVV, is roughly 2–3 weeks for work and study registrations and 3–4 weeks for other cases, counted from your visit date. At the end you receive your personal identity code, and DVV separately decides your municipality of residence.

A practical note on cost: DVV registration as a foreigner is free of charge. If anyone asks you to pay a fee for the henkilötunnus or for registration, that is a red flag.

## Municipality of Residence (Kotikunta): The Part That Actually Unlocks Services

Here is the distinction that catches almost everyone out. Being entered into the Population Information System and receiving a personal identity code is not the same as having a municipality of residence. As InfoFinland puts it, when you receive a personal identity code you are not yet automatically registered as a resident of a specific municipality. DVV makes a separate decision about your kotikunta.

This matters because the kotikunta is what most public services key off. According to DVV and InfoFinland, having a municipality of residence is what gives you:

- The right to use your municipality's services — schools, early childhood education, employment and integration services
- Health and social services through your hyvinvointialue (wellbeing services county), which since 2023 runs public healthcare rather than the municipalities directly
- Eligibility for a Finnish identity card and a Finnish driving licence
- Broadly, the same rights, services, and obligations as a permanent resident

To be assigned a kotikunta, the core requirement is that you have moved to Finland intending to stay for at least one year and are legally resident. On top of that, DVV looks for at least one qualifying ground, such as:

- Citizenship of Finland or another Nordic country
- An EU/EEA citizen's registered right of residence
- A continuous (A) or permanent (P) residence permit
- A family member who already has a Finnish municipality of residence
- A temporary (B) permit valid for at least a year, combined with evidence of a more permanent connection — for example employment or degree studies lasting two or more years

If you do not get a municipality of residence at first — common for people on short or temporary permits — you can be registered in the Population Information System without one, and apply again once your situation becomes more permanent. If you received your personal identity code from Migri or the Tax Administration rather than from a full DVV registration, it is worth confirming with DVV whether a kotikunta has actually been recorded, because that is often the missing piece behind "why can't I book a doctor's appointment."

## Where to Register: Service Points and Help

DVV operates service points across Finland — major cities including Helsinki, Tampere, Turku, and Oulu have offices, and there are around a dozen physical locations nationally. You can also reach DVV by telephone on +358 295 536 320 (Mon–Fri 9–15) and through secure email for questions about your case.

For anyone in the capital region, the standout resource is International House Helsinki (ihhelsinki.fi), a single building where DVV, the Tax Administration, Kela, and other authorities share a service point aimed specifically at international newcomers. It is designed to let you handle registration, tax card, and social-insurance steps in roughly one visit rather than several, and the staff are used to dealing with people in English. Many international employers and universities also have HR or student-services teams who shepherd new arrivals through DVV registration — ask, because they often know the local quirks.

## Keeping Your Registration Current: Notifications of Move

Registration is not a one-time event. Once you have a personal identity code, Finnish law requires you to keep your address current by filing a notification of move (muuttoilmoitus) whenever you move within Finland permanently or temporarily for over 3 months.

The rule, according to DVV, is that you submit the notification at the earliest one month before you move and no later than one week after the move. You can do it online at muuttoil

How Long Does It Take to Get a Personal Identity Code in Finland? - Finland Handbook

# How Long Does It Take to Get a Personal Identity Code in Finland?

 By Finland Handbook Editorial Team June 12, 2026 November 6, 2026 November 6, 2026 

One of the most frustrating "chicken and egg" loops in Finland is trying to open a bank account or sign a rental agreement only to be told you need a Personal Identity Code, while being told by the authorities that the code is currently "in processing." I remember sitting in a cold waiting room in Pasila, clutching my passport and wondering if I’d ever actually exist in the Finnish system. This guide will clarify exactly how long the wait is and how to navigate the administrative silence.

Table of Contents

## Understanding the Personal Identity Code Timelines by Application Path

The time it takes to receive your henkilötunnus (Personal Identity Code) depends almost entirely on which "door" you use to enter the Finnish system. There isn't one single office that handles everyone; rather, your path is determined by your citizenship and your reason for moving. The Finnish Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) has streamlined many digital aspects, but physical identity verification remains a bottleneck that dictates the total duration of your wait.

If you are a non-EU citizen applying for your first residence permit from abroad, you usually request the code as part of your permit application. In this scenario, the code is issued simultaneously with your residence permit. This means your "wait time" for the code is essentially the wait time for your permit, which can range from a few weeks for specialists to several months for family-based ties. The moment you receive your residence permit card, the code is printed on the back. This is by far the most efficient route, as it bypasses the need for a separate visit to the DVV once you land.

However, for EU citizens or those who didn't receive a code with their permit, the process involves a visit to the DVV. In 2026, the standard processing time for a Personal Identity Code at the DVV is generally 1 to 3 weeks after your appointment. The real challenge is often securing the appointment itself. In major cities like Helsinki, Espoo, or Tampere, the "wait for the wait" can be significant. You might find that the first available slot for identity verification is three weeks away, and only after that does the 1–3 week processing clock begin. Understanding Getting Your Personal Identity Code: The Key to Finnish Healthcare is essential here, as this code is the bedrock of your entire administrative life in Finland.

| Application Path | Typical Processing Time | Key Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Residence Permit (Migri) | Linked to permit (1–6 months) | Applied for abroad or at Migri |
| EU Citizen (DVV) | 1–3 weeks after appointment | Valid passport & proof of work/study |
| Nordic Citizen (DVV) | 1 week | Personal appearance at DVV |
| Temporary Worker (Short-term) | 1–2 weeks | Finnish employer's confirmation |

## Factors That Impact the Speed of Your Registration

While the official estimates give a baseline, the reality on the ground in Finland can vary based on seasonal demand. The "August Rush" is a very real phenomenon. Every year, thousands of international students and new hires arrive simultaneously in late summer. If you submit your request in August or early September, expect the DVV processing times to stretch toward the 4-to-6-week mark. Many newcomers get caught in this cycle, struggling to get their electricity contracts or home internet because the system is simply overwhelmed by the volume of new residents.

Another major factor is the completeness of your documentation. The Finnish authorities are meticulous. If you are moving based on family ties, for example, and your marriage certificate or your child’s birth certificate lacks the proper apostille or legalisation, the DVV will pause your application. They won't necessarily tell you immediately; your file might just sit in a "pending" queue until a clerk reviews it and sends a request for clarification. This can add weeks to the process. Always ensure your documents are translated into Finnish, Swedish, or English by an authorized translator before your appointment.

Furthermore, your location in Finland matters. While Helsinki is the hub, it is also the most congested. If you have the flexibility to travel, sometimes booking an appointment at a DVV office in a smaller town like Porvoo, Lahti, or even further afield can shave weeks off your wait for an appointment. Once the identity verification is done, the digital processing time is relatively uniform across the country, but getting that face-to-face meeting is the primary hurdle. Many people overlook how critical this step is when Registering Your Move (Muuttoilmoitus) with DVV and Posti to ensure their address is correctly linked to their new code.

## Navigating Life and Health Without a Code

The most pressing question for most is: what do I do while I wait? It feels like life is on hold. You cannot easily get a Finnish bank account, which in turn means you cannot get "Strong Electronic Identification" (bank IDs) to log into government services. During this gap, you are in a state of administrative limbo. For everyday needs, you can often use your foreign passport for basic things, but for services like healthcare, it becomes tricky. Public health centers usually require a Personal Identity Code to create a patient record in their digital systems.

If you fall ill during this waiting period, you might wonder Can I See a Doctor in Finland Before I Get a Municipality of Residence? The answer is yes, but it is often more complicated and expensive. Without the code and the subsequent "Municipality of Residence" (kotikunta) status, you are often billed at the full cost of care rather than the subsidized resident rate. This is where having private bridge insurance is a lifesaver. Companies like Cigna Global or SafetyWing are popular choices for expats who are caught in the "waiting for DVV" phase. These providers allow you to access private clinics like Terveystalo or Mehiläinen without needing a Finnish ID code.

While waiting for your code, SafetyWing can provide travel-medical style coverage that handles emergencies, while Cigna Global offers more comprehensive annual plans that cover you while you are still invisible to the Finnish Kela system. Using private care during these first few weeks is often the only way to avoid the stress of navigating the public system without a code. It’s also worth noting that until you have that code, you won't be able to easily use Omakanta and the Kanta Services: Finland's Digital Health Records and Prescriptions, as these require Finnish bank IDs to log in. Keeping your private insurance details handy is the best way to ensure you aren't left stranded.

## Practical Steps to Speed Up the Process

To ensure you get your code as fast as possible, you need to be proactive rather than reactive. The moment you know your move-in date, or the moment you receive your residence permit, check the DVV’s online booking system. Do not wait until you land in Finland to see what’s available. Appointments fill up weeks in advance. If you see no appointments in Helsinki, widen your search radius. The train system in Finland is excellent, and a one-hour trip to a neighboring town could save you three weeks of waiting in the city.

When you attend your appointment, bring every possible document that proves your right to be in Finland. This includes your passport, your residence permit card (if applicable), your employment contract, or your certificate of attendance from a university. For EU citizens, proving your "right of residence" often requires showing that you have sufficient funds or a job. If the clerk has everything they need in one go, your application can be processed in the "fast track" queue. If they have to ask for more info, you go back to the bottom of the pile.

Once you have your code, your next step is often Getting Your Personal Identity Code: The Key to Finnish Healthcare by ensuring your municipality of residence is also registered. The code itself is just a string of numbers; the status attached to it (whether you are a permanent resident or a temporary visitor) determines your rights to Kela benefits and public healthcare. If you are a student, for example, you should clarify Can I Use Finnish Healthcare on a Student Residence Permit? as your access level might differ from someone on a permanent work contract. Once the code arrives via post or email, treat it like gold—it is the master key to your new life.

## Managing Your Healthcare Transition

As you wait for the administrative wheels to turn, it's vital to have a plan for your prescriptions and ongoing health needs. Many expats make the mistake of assuming they can just walk into a pharmacy with a foreign prescription and get their meds. In Finland, pharmacies generally require a Finnish electronic prescription. Until you have your Personal Identity Code and can be entered into the system, getting a Finnish doctor to issue that prescription is your first priority. Again, this is where private providers like Cigna Global or SafetyWing facilitate faster access to private doctors who can bridge that gap for you.

Once you finally receive your code, you can begin the process of Healthcare in Finland for Foreign Residents: The Complete System Guide (2027). This involves registering at your local terveysasema (health station). Don't expect this to happen automatically. Even after the DVV gives you a code, you often need to proactively contact your local wellbeing services county to ensure you are in their database. This is a common point of confusion: the DVV manages your identity, but the Wellbeing Services County manages your health access.

Finally, keep in mind that the Personal Identity Code is also the prerequisite for applying for a Kela card. You can read more about this in Kela Explained: Health Insurance, Reimbursements, and Your Kela Card. Without the ID code, Kela cannot process your application for social security coverage. If you are working, your employer will also need this code to pay your salary and handle your tax withholdings correctly. It truly is the "linchpin" of the Finnish system. While the 1-to-3-week wait might feel like an eternity when you're trying to settle in, being prepared with private insurance like SafetyWing or Cigna Global ensures that your health and safety aren't compromised by a bit of bureaucratic lag.

Location: Wyoming, USA | Email: contact@choismedia.com

| 5 | Get a verokortti (tax card) | Vero (Tax Administration) |

...

| 8 | Register as a jobseeker if you have no work | Your municipality’s employment services |

...

EU citizens staying more than three months register their right of residence with Migri within three months of arrival, only after moving, for 53 euros. Nordic citizens instead register in person at DVV within one month of moving if they stay more than six months. Permit holders get a residence permit card, delivered to a collection point in Finland within about two weeks of the decision; it is not an identity document.

In Helsinki one address covers most of week one. International House Helsinki, at Ratapihantie 7 in Pasila since 1 June 2026, handles EU registration for Migri, the code and municipality of residence for DVV, the tax card for Vero, jobseeker registration and Kela by remote service, Monday to Friday 9.00–16.00. Identity cards are the exception: newcomers go to the Helsinki Police Department at Pasilanraitio 11. Espoo and Vantaa residents use the same house, because DVV’s Espoo office has closed permanently.

...

## Weeks two to four: what needs the personal identity code

If Migri grants you a residence permit, EU registration or a residence card, you are registered automatically and the code comes with the decision. Otherwise you request it from DVV with an online form and visit in person within one month, every family member included; it is free and takes two to three weeks in work and study cases. Tax offices in larger cities issue codes for tax purposes only, usually within one to three business days. Neither of those codes gives you a municipality of residence – for that you still apply to DVV, as part 3 explains.

| Task | Code needed? | What applies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prepaid SIM card | No | Sold at R-kiosks and supermarkets; no address needed either |
| Registering as a jobseeker | Yes, in practice | Job Market Finland asks for a DVV extract or Kela card as proof; non-EU citizens also need a valid residence permit |
| Bank account | Yes, in practice | The bank needs your name, code and address; a driving licence is not accepted as ID |
| Online banking codes | Yes | A bank may refuse them if you have no code or are not in the Population Information System |
| Kela benefits and the Kela card | Yes, plus a bank account | Kela pays nothing in cash |
| Contract phone subscription | Yes, plus an address | A credit check follows; otherwise you pay in advance |

sources.title: Streamlined services for issuing personal identity codes and municipality of residence for foreign citizens - Finnish Government
highlights:
The Digital and Population Data Services Agency took action last year in order to streamline the registration of foreigners. You can now get your personal identity code when visiting the agency in 12 locations. The updated website and instructional videos will guide customers to use services that match their situation.

The registration of foreigners' personal data has accelerated as the Digital and Population Data Services Agency has improved its practices and systems. You can now apply for a personal identity code and municipality of residence online, which speeds up processing and improves the accuracy of the data. After filling in the online form, the customer must still usually visit the agency in order to verify their identity.

“D ... We are now able to provide a personal identity code and a municipality of residence during a visit, provided the conditions are met,” says Maisa Gynther, Chief Specialist at the Digital and Population Data Services Agency.

...

A few service locations of the Digital and Population Data Services Agency tested the practice first and started issuing a personal identity code during a personal visit, and as their experiences were positive, the practice was adopted permanently. At the moment, persons who have booked an appointment and completed an online form may receive their personal identity code in 12 locations: Helsinki, Joensuu, Jyväskylä, Kuopio, Lahti, Lappeenranta, Oulu, Pori, Rovaniemi, Tampere, Turku and Vaasa. 

To receive their personal identity code during the visit, the customer must first submit their data to the Digital and Population Data Services Agency using an online form and book an appointment online. They must also meet the requirements for obtaining a personal identity code. However, a personal identity code cannot always be issued during a visit if the matter requires further clarification. 

The online form for obtaining a personal identity code is available to all foreigners, and it does not require strong identification. You can use the same form to request a municipality of residence if you are intending to stay in Finland for more than one year. The conditions for obtaining a personal identity code and municipality of residence are examined individually for each customer.

sources.title: Finnish Personal Identity Code (Henkilötunnus) Guide | NordicExpat
highlights:
### Step 1: Submit the Online Form

Start at dvv.fi/en/foreigner-registration, which links to the registration form at lomakkeet.dvv.fi. No login or strong authentication is required to submit it. You provide your personal details, your reason for staying in Finland, and contact information. Parents submit one separate form per child under 18. (A paper form exists if you genuinely cannot use the online one.)

### Step 2: Book and Attend an In-Person Appointment

After submitting the form, book an appointment at a DVV service point and attend within one month. When booking you choose:

- Book for one person if registering only yourself.
- Book for multiple people or a family if there are 2–5 people; for six or more, book two appointments.

Everyone being registered must attend in person, including children — there is no way around the identity verification.

### Step 3: Bring the Right Documents

Take with you:

- Valid passport or official EU/EEA photo ID card.
- Residence permit card (non-EU) or EU registration certificate — or proof you have applied for one.
- Proof of legal grounds for staying: employment contract, study acceptance/enrolment certificate, or equivalent.
- Proof of a Finnish address if you have it: a rental agreement, or confirmation from your employer or university.
- For family relationships, bring legalised and translated certificates (marriage, birth) where relevant.

### Step 4: Wait for Processing

DVV processes the request after your visit. According to DVV, expect roughly:

...

- Other applications: about 3–4 weeks.

...

This is the single most common misunderstanding, so treat it as a separate fact: having a henkilötunnus is not the same as having a municipality of residence (kotikunta — "home municipality"). The personal identity code identifies you; the kotikunta status is what entitles you to subsidised municipal and wellbeing-county services — most importantly public healthcare at standard client fees, and day care.

Both DVV and Migri are explicit that getting a code does not automatically give you a kotikunta. You apply for the municipality of residence separately with DVV, and eligibility depends on factors like the nature and length of your stay. If you register in person with DVV, raise the kotikunta question at the same appointment so you do not leave thinking you are covered for healthcare when you are not. For the wider registration picture, see our guide to registering with DVV.

...

## Common Problems and Fixes

- "My permit was granted but I never got a code." Automatic issuance needs your identity to have been verified by a Finnish authority and your details to match your passport exactly. If it did not happen, request the code from DVV in person after you arrive — do not wait for it to appear on its own.
- "I have a henkilötunnus but the health centre says I'm not covered." You almost certainly have the code but not a kotikunta. Apply for the municipality of residence with DVV; until then, non-emergency public care may not be available at subsidised rates.
- "My name is spelled wrong / my date of birth is incorrect." Errors trace back to the source documents and identity check. Contact DVV to correct registered details; in narrow cases the code itself can be changed (e.g. wrong date of birth recorded).
- "I couldn't get a DVV appointment within a month of submitting the form." Appointment availability varies by city and season. Book as early as you can; if slots are scarce, check service points in nearby municipalities and the booking system at different times of day.
- "A bank refused me because I only have a foreigner's identity number." That is expected — it is not a full henkilötunnus. Use a Wise or Revolut account as interim banking, and apply for the full code once you qualify.

...

- DVV — foreigner registration: the form, appointment booking, and document list — dvv.fi/en/foreigner-registration
- Migri — personal identity code with a residence permit: how the automatic process works — migri.fi/en/personal-identity-code
- InfoFinland — after you arrive: plain-language newcomer overview of registration steps — infofinland.fi
- International House Helsinki: a one-stop service point covering DVV registration, tax, and Kela for the Helsinki region — ihhelsinki.fi
- Your employer or university: many international employers and universities have staff who walk new arrivals through DVV registration.

sources.title: GUIDE: What to do after moving to Finland
highlights:
#### 2 Visit International House Helsinki

- Visit International House Helsinki (or similar services in other cities).

- At the local registry office dvv.fi, register to get:

*Henkilötunnus (SNN, personal identity code) – your personal identifier in all government systems (similar to a tax identification number). This number consists of six digits of your birth date and four additional characters. It's issued for free, and processing can take from 30 minutes to two weeks. To obtain it, you need a residential address. Even if your Social Security Number is already on the back of your residence permit card, you still need to visit the DVV to get a paper extract from the registry. *Kotikunta – registration of your municipality, where you plan to live, pay taxes, and receive services. A temporary apartment with a postal address (but not a hotel) is enough. You can also list your office address, and your company may assist with this. 

- Get a tax card at the tax office (vero.fi). This is an A4 sheet that shows your tax percentage. It’s issued for free on the day of application. If you already have a Social Security Number, you can order it by phone.

- At Kela, submit applications for:

— Kela card – a plastic social security card that simplifies identification at clinics. The card will be mailed to you within ~3 months, but you can access public healthcare immediately after submitting the application. — E uropean Health Insurance Card – similar but valid across Europe. — Child benefits. — Other benefits.

#### 3 Visit the police

Visit the police and apply for an ID card (henkilökortti). Once you receive an email from DVV confirming you’ve obtained your henkilötunnus and kotikunta, you can go to the police to get your ID card. Either schedule an appointment or wait in line. Bring a photo with you.

...

Open a bank account and request bank authorization codes. It's better to go to the bank after receiving your ID card from the police, as they will open the account on the same day. You can apply for an account at several banks at once. Popular banks: 

- S-Pankki
- OP (requires a permanent address)

...

Even if you’re moving soon, provide the bank with the registered DVV address. It’s easier to request mail forwarding from Posti than to wait 20 days for a DVV address change and then go to the bank.

sources.title: Your First Week in Finland: An Arrival Checklist | NordicExpat
highlights:
Before you plan your week, understand the single fact that shapes it: almost nothing official in Finland works without a henkilötunnus (the Finnish personal identity code). Your online banking codes, your tax card, your Kela registration, and most online government services all expect that code. It is issued by the DVV (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency) when you register, and registration involves an in-person appointment.

...

Get a phone connection. A working Finnish or local number matters more than it sounds, because so many later steps — bank onboarding, OmaVero login, two-factor codes — assume you can receive an SMS. Prepaid SIM cards are widely sold at convenience kiosks (such as R-kioski), supermarkets, and operator stores from DNA, Elisa, and Telia. If you would rather arrive already connected, an eSIM bought before you fly (for example through Airalo) gives you data

...

Sort out getting around. In the greater Helsinki area, public transport runs on HSL (Helsingin seudun liikenne). You do not need a travel card to start moving: the free HSL app sells single tickets and short day tickets without even an account, and you can tap a contactless bank card or phone on board many services. The HSL area is divided into zones labelled A to E, so check which zones your trips cover before you buy. Fares are adjusted periodically, so treat any euro figure you see online as indicative and check the current price in the app or at hsl.fi.

...

This is the keystone task. Registration with DVV is what produces your personal identity code and, where you qualify, your municipality of residence.

The process has two parts. First, submit the foreigner registration form online at dvv.fi/en/foreigner-registration. You can complete this before your appointment to speed things along. Second, book and attend an in-person appointment at a DVV service point. Everyone who requests a personal identity code must appear in person.

Bring originals, not copies:

- A valid passport or official photo ID card
- Your residence permit card (non-EU) or your EU registration certificate, or proof you have applied for one
- Proof of your legal grounds for staying — typically an employment contract or a letter of acceptance from a Finnish institution
- Proof of your Finnish address, if you have it

Processing times vary, so book your appointment as early in your first week as the calendar allows.

...

That is a deliberately high default, and the only way to avoid it is to get a tax card in place before your first payday.

Once you have a personal identity code, you can order a tax card with Vero's form 5042e (if you are staying more than six months) or through OmaVero, the online tax service at vero.fi (logging in needs a mobile certificate, certificate card or online banking codes), and give it to your employer. Ask your employer how much in advance they need it (Vero's guide is approximately 2 weeks before payday), so the moment your code comes through, this should jump to the top of your list. If your code has not arrived yet but you are about to start work, ask whether a tax office near you can issue a personal identity code, so you are not stuck on the 60% rate. Newcomers in the capital region can also get tax guidance in person at International House Helsinki, which co-locates DVV, tax, and Kela services.

sources.title: A foreigner can apply for a personal identity code and municipality of residence online - Finnish Government
highlights:
The everyday life of a foreigner moving to Finland is made easier when their details are registered in the Population Information System. The Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) maintains this information and has now made it possible for a foreigner to apply for a personal identity code and municipality of residence online. If you fill in the online form before you go in person, it is easier to obtain your personal identity code and municipality of residence.

The online forms for applying for a personal identity code and municipality of residence are available to all foreigners and do not require strong identification to fill them in. Once a foreigner has submitted an application for a personal identity code or municipality of residence online, they usually also have to visit the Digital and Population Digital Services Agency in person. The conditions for obtaining a personal identity code and municipality of residence are examined individually for each customer.

A new online form to apply for a personal identity code is being introduced on 13 May 2024. The submission of the preliminary information in digital format allows the customer's case to be dealt with more quickly during a customer service visit. The Digital and Population Data Services Agency Is piloting the provision of personal identity codes during customer service visits in some municipalities during the summer. This is possible for customers who have filled in the online form and made an appointment in advance in Helsinki, Turku, Tampere, Jyväskylä and Oulu.

sources.title: DVV Registration in Finland 2026: Identity Code | ENB
highlights:
Many residence-permit applicants receive a personal identity code during the Migri process and it appears on the permit card. If not, it can be requested through DVV foreigner registration; in some work/tax cases Vero can also be involved in issuing a code.

DVV registration requires reliable identity and a genuine Finnish connection. Passport/official ID, residence status and work/study/family documents may be required.

...

After submitting the municipality-of-residence form, follow DVV's confirmation instructions. The current form requires many applicants to visit a DVV service location in person within one month.

Keep a valid passport/ID and original documents supporting the application ground ready for identity verification. Booking before arrival can reduce delays.
